title: Kernel Credit Accounting & Fairness Playbook
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes the design, configuration, operational runbooks, and rollout guidance for the kernel-level credit accounting and fairness layer used in Redwood’s multi-tenant inference runtime. The system ensures predictable throughput and latency SLOs while preventing noisy-tenant and priority-inversion problems when many concurrent requests contend for GPU kernels and KV-cache resources.

Intended audience
-----------------
- Runtime engineers (owners of kernel scheduler and admission control)
- SREs on-call for serving clusters
- Capacity planners and product owners for Dedicated/Private products

Goals and non-goals
-------------------
Goals:
- Provide stable latency for high-priority routes while allowing best-effort capacity for trial/metered users
- Bound tail latency by limiting long queue accumulation on kernel execution paths
- Offer explainable and auditable per-customer accounting for GPU kernel usage

Non-goals:
- Replace higher-level rate-limiters or API quotas (this works below API surface in serving runtime)
- Fully eliminate all client-visible variability in extreme overloads — we provide graceful degradation strategies instead

Definitions and key concepts
----------------------------
- Credit: abstract unit representing entitlement to consume a kernel timeslice. Credits are consumed when a request enters a kernel-execution critical section.
- Credit Bucket: per-tenant (and per-priority) balance tracked in-memory (and periodically checkpointed).
- Refill policy: rate at which credits are added to a bucket (tokens/sec).
- Debit event: decrement of credits on kernel entry; if insufficient credits, request is queued or subject to degradation depending on policy.
- Fairness window: configurable sliding window (default 60s) for measuring usage and computing deficits.

Architecture overview
---------------------
1) Placement: The credit accounting layer sits in the local serving process before kernel invocation and is enforced per-shard (NUMA / GPU device). It integrates with:
   - admission-controller (global decisions for burst allowances),
   - kernel-mapper (selects kernel variant after accounting), and
   - request-pool (local queues and backpressure).
2) Persistence: Buckets are ephemeral but periodically checkpointed to the control plane to enable cross-node rebalancing and debugging. Checkpoint sync is best-effort every 30s; immediate sync occurs on tenant migration.
3) Telemetry: metrics exported as Prometheus/OTel metrics and traces. See "Telemetry and dashboards" section.

Fairness algorithm (summary)
---------------------------
We use a hybrid Deficit-Weighted Round Robin (DWRR) with a decay term to prefer recent underutilization. Highlights:
- Each tenant t has a configured weight w_t and min-guarantee g_t (credits/sec).
- Deficit increases by w_t * quantum on each scheduling round and decays at half-life configured via fairness-window.
- When kernel resources are scarce, tenants with exhausted deficits are deprioritized.
- Priorities (system, paid-enterprise, paid-standard, trial) are mapped to weight ranges and short-term burst credits.

Configuration reference (example)
--------------------------------
(Stored in runtime config: /etc/redwood/runtime/kernel-crediting.yaml per node)

---
# Top-level config version
version: 1
default_fairness_window_seconds: 60
quantum_micros: 5000  # scheduling quantum used to bump deficit
priority_classes:
  system:
    weight: 100
    min_guarantee: 1000
    burst_tokens: 5000
    preemptible: false
  enterprise:
    weight: 50
    min_guarantee: 300
    burst_tokens: 1000
    preemptible: false
  standard:
    weight: 10
    min_guarantee: 50
    burst_tokens: 200
    preemptible: true
  trial:
    weight: 1
    min_guarantee: 5
    burst_tokens: 50
    preemptible: true
tenant_overrides:  # per-tenant config (optional)
  tenant-abc123:
    weight: 20
    min_guarantee: 100

Operational runbook: high-level flow
-----------------------------------
1) Admission: incoming request -> admission controller -> credit check.
2) If credits >= kernel_cost(request) -> debit and enqueue for kernel mapper.
3) If credits < kernel_cost -> check fallback policy:
   a) If low-priority and degradation allowed -> route to a quantized model variant (lower kernel cost).
   b) If burst_allowed (and bucket has burst_tokens) -> consume burst tokens and admit.
   c) Else -> return 429 with Retry-After or queue with bounded wait (configurable max_wait_ms).
4) On kernel completion, an accounting reconciliation event returns partial credits for short-circuited operations (e.g., cache hit avoids kernel).

Runbook: incident scenarios and steps
------------------------------------
A. Symptom: sudden increase in p99 latency on standard and trial tenants while enterprise remains stable
- Likely cause: burst tokens exhausted or noisy tenant consuming more than weight.
- Steps:
  1. Run quick telemetry queries (below) to identify tenant with spike in kernel_invocations.
  2. Inspect credit_balance and deficit for top-10 tenants.
  3. If noisy-tenant found, temporarily set tenant weight to a lower value:
     redwoodctl runtime update-tenant-config --tenant tenant-id --weight 5
  4. If more immediate relief needed, toggle preemption threshold to allow enterprise preemption:
     redwoodctl runtime set-flag --name preemption_aggressiveness --value high
  5. Document incident and add tenant to noisy-tenant watchlist.

B. Symptom: large queue growth observed on particular GPU device
- Likely cause: NUMA hotspot, slow kernel variant or memory thrashing.
- Steps:
  1. Correlate queue growth with kernel time/per-kernel-error.
  2. Offload trial/standard queues by increasing min_guarantee for enterprise/system or disable burst for low tier.
  3. If kernel is hung, trigger per-device kill and warmstart per runbook: /eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/numa-aware-shard-placement-eviction-playbook-2026.json

Telemetry and dashboards (queries and metrics)
--------------------------------------------
Core metrics (Prometheus names):
- redwood_kernel_credit_balance{tenant,priority} (gauge, credits)
- redwood_kernel_deficit{tenant,priority} (gauge, credits)
- redwood_kernel_debits_total (counter)
- redwood_kernel_preemptions_total (counter)
- redwood_kernel_burst_tokens_consumed_total (counter)
- redwood_kernel_queue_length{device} (gauge)
- redwood_kernel_wait_time_seconds_bucket (histogram)
- redwood_kernel_success_rate{tenant} (gauge)

Sample alert rules (SRE):
- Alert: KernelQueueHigh
  Expr: avg_over_time(redwood_kernel_queue_length[1m]) > 50 for 2m
  Severity: P2
- Alert: TenantCreditDepletedHigh
  Expr: increase(redwood_kernel_debits_total{tenant=~".*"}[5m]) > (tenant_expected_rate * 3) and redwood_kernel_credit_balance < 10
  Severity: P3

Suggested dashboards:
- Credit health (per-priority): median/95/99 balances, deficits, burst consumption
- Fairness score: measured as max(usage_weight_ratio, enforced_deficit_ratio) over 5m window (explainable metric for SLAs)
- Kernel queue and preemptions by device and shard

Benchmarks and expected behavior
--------------------------------
Run benchmark harness (benchmarking-and-perf-suite/mixed-workload-slo-simulation-suite) with the following scenarios to validate fairness config changes:
- Scenario A: 80% enterprise, 20% trial traffic — expected p99 for enterprise < 120ms, trial p99 degraded but < 500ms.
- Scenario B: Noisy-tenant flood (10x normal) — system should cap noisy tenant to < 2x its guaranteed throughput within fairness window.
- Scenario C: Cold-start heavy KV-cache misses — verify that debit refunds occur on cache hit avoidance and that observed token consumption aligns with kernel-time.

Configuration change and rollout checklist
----------------------------------------
- Author change in a feature branch of runtime config repo.
- Unit tests for deficit logic and decay.
- Integration tests using local benchmark harness that covers: single-device stress, multi-device distributed run, and migration scenario.
- Canary rollout (20% nodes) with aggressive telemetry watch for 24h.
- Gradual ramp to 100% over 48h.
- Post-rollout: run fairness regression tests from benchmark suite and record artifacts.

APIs and CLI examples
--------------------
1) Query tenant credit balance:
   curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://runtime.internal/api/v1/tenants/tenant-abc123/credits
   Response: {"balance": 310, "deficit": 120, "last_refill_ts": "2026-02-14T09:34:12Z"}

2) Update tenant weight:
   redwoodctl runtime update-tenant-config --tenant tenant-abc123 --weight 20 --min-guarantee 100

3) Toggle node-level flag:
   redwoodctl runtime set-flag --name crediting_enabled --value true --nodes node-12,node-13

Debugging snippets (common queries)
----------------------------------
- Top 10 tenants by kernel debits in last 5m
  PromQL: topk(10, increase(redwood_kernel_debits_total[5m]))
- Per-device queue growth with tenant breakdown
  PromQL: sum by (device, tenant) (increase(redwood_kernel_queue_length[5m]))

Known limitations and caveats
---------------------------
- Checkpointing is best-effort; a node crash can cause temporary mismatch between observed usage and control-plane records. Use reconciliation script (tools/runtime/reconcile_credits.py) after node replacement.
- Small tenants with burst allowances may intermittently exceed long-term share; careful billing/visibility is required to prevent surprises.
- Very large model kernel variance: when kernel cost estimators are inaccurate, tenant accounting may under- or over-charge. Ensure model_cost_estimator is profiled for new model variants.

Safety and privacy considerations
--------------------------------
- Tenant ids in telemetry are hashed at rest in long-term stores. Short-term debugging dashboards will display tenant ids unmasked only to engineers with the "runtime-debug" permission.
- Audit logs are generated for any manual tenant-config changes and stored for 365 days (see security-and-compliance/audit-logging).

Appendix A: Example fairness math (simple view)
------------------------------------------------
Let quantum Q=100, weight w_t for tenant t. Deficit D_t increases by Q*w_t each round and decays at rate r per second. A tenant can run when D_t >= cost_k (cost in credits). On run, D_t -= cost_k.
Decay: D_t = D_t * exp(-ln2 / half_life_seconds) every second (half-life parameterizable).

Appendix B: Troubleshooting checklist (quick)
--------------------------------------------
- If p99 latency spikes: check credit_balance and kernel_queue_length -> reduce burst or reduce noisy tenant weight.
- If sustained undershoot of enterprise guarantees: increase min_guarantee and observe for 10m.
- If frequent preemptions observed: lower preemption_aggressiveness and add more quota to enterprise/system.
